children: Australia will produce 29.9 million metric tons of wheat this year, the government projected on Tuesday, lifting its forecast by a little over 3 million tons following better-than-expected rainfall in many cropping areas.

The extra tons from Australia, the world's third-biggest wheat exporter, will add supply to a global market that has tightened in recent months, driving prices to their highest level since early 2023.

The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES), part of the agriculture ministry, also in a quarterly crop report raised its forecast for Australia's barley harvest by more than 2 million tons to 16.4 million tons and for canola production by just over 1 million tons to 7.3 million tons.

Australia will still reap around 6 million tons less wheat than last year — in part due to an 11% decrease in the amount of land sown — putting the harvest roughly in line with the average of the last 10 seasons, ABARES said.
Production of barley and canola — which growers preferred to wheat because they promised better margins — will be only slightly lower than last year and around one-third above their 10-year averages.
ABARES said growing conditions were excellent in South Australia, Victoria and southern New South Wales but average in Western Australia and poor in northern New South Wales and Queensland.
The year began much drier and with the threat of fertiliser shortages and a powerful El Niño weather event — something that often limits rainfall.
"Seasonal conditions throughout winter have been much better than expected, boosting production prospects across most major southern cropping regions," ABARES said.
High fertiliser prices had also had a smaller impact than expected, it added.
Four analysts said last week they expected Australia to produce between 30 and 32 million tons of wheat this year, slightly above ABARES' forecast.

ABARES said production of summer crops sorghum, cotton and rice – which are grown in New South Wales and Queensland — would fall by between 22% and 34% in the coming season due to lack of soil moisture and irrigation water.
